doc.title: Jon Hendricks interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Pitching vocalese and the Manhattan Transfer story
summary: Defines vocalese as lyrics telling a story; recalls meeting Tim Hauser and helping Manhattan Transfer.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well I tell them that the most popular exponents of it, therefore the best known, are the Manhattan Transfer. And they all say, “oh yeah, the Manhattan Transfer, oh yeah we know them.” This is what happened around the table. And this one lady says, “oh I have all their albums.” I said, “well do you have the album ‘Vocalese’?” They said, “oh yeah, that was their biggest seller.” I says, “yeah, I wrote that album.”

And then I tell them the story of the formation of the Manhattan Transfer. Their idea was to be a group like Lambert, Hendricks & Ross. That’s why I helped them. That was their aim. I met Tim Hauser in a taxi. He was a taxi driver. And I got in his cab with my brother. And he says, “I know you, you’re Jon Hendricks.” I said, “how do you know me?” He says, “I know you. My name is Tim Hauser and my girlfriend Janis Siegel and I live in Brooklyn and we’re going to start a Lambert, Hendricks & Ross type group called Manhattan Transfer.” I gave him my card, and I said, “any time I can help you, let me know.” And that was how they started. I said so that’s what vocalese is. It’s the setting of lyrics to established American jazz instrumentals in a form so that it tells a story with a beginning, a middle, an end, a plot, a cast of characters, the horns become the characters, and they make a commentary on the subject matter which is determined by the title. “Jumpin’ at the Woodside” becomes a dissertation on a hotel where jazz musicians could stay and play at any time because there was nobody to complain because everybody staying there is also a jazz musician. So what do they care if you rehearse all night. They’re probably rehearsing all night. So that’s what that was. And each of the horn players makes some kind of comment on that. Buck Clayton has the trumpet solo, Lester Young a tenor solo, and Basie on piano. And all this has to work like an opera or like a well constructed theater piece, like a drama. Each person has to be a character within a previously defined plot structure, which is determined by the title. So it contains elements of theater, of literature, and above all, of poetry, and even above that, philosophy. So it’s a completely new form, but it’s based on the depths of the old established forms, mainly philosophy and poetry. Then they sit up and take notice.
Yeah, right. You summed it up. That’s great.
